Before we start

After importing data, we usually have to bring it into the right shape before we can analyse it. In these exercises we reshape a data set, clean it, merge it with a second one and summarise the result.

Write your code in an R script saved in 2026_Data_Handling/exercises/code, for example exercise_05.R. Open your RStudio project first. Type the code rather than copying it, and read every error message. If something does not work, raise your hand.

Exercise What we do
1 Reshaping: from wide to long and back
2 Cleaning: mutate(), filter() and select()
3 Merging two data sets and summarising the result
Training Tidying a small table, and correlations across years

The data. There is nothing to download. We use the economics data set from the ggplot2 package, and we create the other data sets with the code shown below. Start with:

library(tidyverse)

Exercise 1: reshaping data

economics contains monthly data on several indicators of the US economy:

Variable Description
date month of data collection
pce personal consumption expenditures (billions of USD)
pop total population (thousands)
psavert personal savings rate (percent)
uempmed median duration of unemployment (weeks)
unemploy number of unemployed (thousands)

  1. Inspect the data with head(), dim() and range() on date. How many rows and columns are there, and which period is covered? Is the data in long or in wide format?

  2. Reshape the data into long format with pivot_longer(), so that for each date there is one row per variable. Save the result as df_long. How many rows do you expect before you run the code?

  3. Reshape df_long back to wide format with pivot_wider() and save it as df. Check that df has the same dimensions and column names as economics.

  4. Give one task for which the long format is more convenient, and one for which the wide format is.

Exercise 2: cleaning and preparing data

  1. Add a variable unemployment_rate to df, the number of unemployed (unemploy) divided by the total population (pop). Is this the unemployment rate you read about in the news?

  2. Extract the year from date with year() from the lubridate package and save it in df as a new variable called year.

  3. We are only interested in observations collected after the year 2000, that is from 2001 on. Filter df accordingly and save the result as df_reduced. What is the first date left?

  4. We are now only interested in the evolution of pce and pop over time. Keep date, pce and pop in df_reduced.

  5. Add an indicator variable after_2000 to df that is TRUE for observations after the year 2000 and FALSE otherwise. Count both groups. Why would this variable be of no use in df_reduced?

Exercise 3: merging data

We also use quarterly US GDP data from 2013 to 2017, obtained from FRED. Create it with:

gdp <- data.frame(
  date = seq(as.Date("2013-01-01"), as.Date("2017-10-01"), by = "quarter"),
  gdp = c(16648.189, 16728.687, 16953.838, 17192.019,
          17197.738, 17518.508, 17804.228, 17912.079,
          18063.529, 18279.784, 18401.626, 18435.137,
          18525.933, 18711.702, 18892.639, 19089.379,
          19280.084, 19438.643, 19692.595, 20037.088)
)

  1. We want to merge df with gdp. Which one should be the left table, and which one the right table? What is the joining variable? Which problems do you foresee?

  2. Merge them with left_join() and save the result as df_left. How many rows does it have?

  3. The variable gdp has missing values. Count them and explain where they come from. Propose a way to get a data set that is useful for an analysis of both variables.

  4. Now merge with inner_join() and save the result as df_inner. How does it differ from df_left? Which one would you use in practice?

  5. Which rows of gdp have no partner in df? Use anti_join().

  6. Starting from df_inner, create a table summary_stats with the mean, median and standard deviation of unemployment_rate and gdp per year, plus the number of observations. Use group_by() and summarise(). What do you observe?

  7. Arrange summary_stats by year in descending order.

Additional exercises for training

Exercise 4: tidy the pregnancy data

The following table contains pregnancy counts in a population:

preg <- tribble(
  ~pregnant, ~male, ~female,
  "yes", NA, 10,
  "no", 20, 12
)

  1. Is the data set tidy? What are the variables?

  2. Tidy preg. Do you need pivot_longer() or pivot_wider()?

  3. What does the missing value stand for here, and what would you do with it?

Exercise 5: correlations across countries and years

The code below simulates data on four countries: an index of Covid cases and the public spending on fighting Covid, in 2020 and 2021. The data is simulated and says nothing about reality. set.seed() makes sure that we all draw the same numbers.

set.seed(3230)
covid <- data.frame(Country = c("US", "DE", "CH", "FR"),
                    Covid_2020 = runif(4, 0, 1),
                    AntiCovidExpenses_2020 = runif(4, 500, 1000))
covid <- cbind(covid,
  Covid_2021 = covid$Covid_2020 + rnorm(4, 0, 0.1),
  AntiCovidExpenses_2021 = covid$AntiCovidExpenses_2020 + rnorm(4, 0, 100))

  1. Is this data set in long or in wide format?

  2. You want the correlation between spending and cases across countries and years. Reshape the data so that you can compute it. Look at names_to = c(".value", "year") and names_sep in ?pivot_longer.

  3. Compute the correlation with cor(). How much can you conclude from it?
